bp: Crowdsourced labeling is the work behind many machine learning systems: people mark images, text, audio, or video so a later model can learn what counts as the right answer. The platform has a practical problem before any algorithm appears. It needs many workers, but it cannot treat every submitted label as equally helpful. Some workers are careful, some are inexperienced, and some may deliberately submit bad labels or try to earn payment with minimal effort. If bad labels enter the training pile, the later model learns from corrupted examples. If the platform punishes too harshly, honest workers may avoid participating. This paper serves that tension. It proposes a Negativity-Aware Incentive mechanism for paying and penalizing workers according to whether their actual labeling behavior helps or harms the final data quality, with reported deployment evidence from NetEase Youling.
wh: The hard part is that label quality is both a measurement problem and a human incentives problem. A platform does not directly observe effort or honesty; it sees submitted answers, worker history, task difficulty, and later agreement or result quality. Existing methods, according to the abstract, often ignore fraud or assume worker utility is never negative. That means they can reward good work but have trouble assigning real cost to harmful work. Yet penalty design is dangerous. If every mistake is treated as fraud, new or lower-ability workers may leave. If no mistake carries a cost, malicious or careless workers can damage the dataset while still being paid. The system must therefore separate helpful from harmful contribution, attach money to that separation, and keep the rule fair enough that ordinary workers still want to join. It also has to work across different media types and at real platform scale.
naive: A smart beginner would pay workers per completed task and remove workers who fail too many gold-standard checks. That is simple and easy to explain. It fails because completion is not the same as contribution. A worker can submit many labels that look complete while adding noise or fraud. Another beginner plan is to pay according to average accuracy. That helps, but it can miss the effect of a specific worker on a specific task result, especially when task difficulty and worker ability differ. A third plan is to apply fixed fines for bad answers. That can discourage fraud, but it can also scare off honest workers who make occasional mistakes or face harder items.
ap: The core idea is to make contribution signed: a worker can add value, add little value, or subtract value. The paper's Ability-Result Characteristic Function combines two pieces of evidence, the worker's ability and the real-time task result, to define how much that worker contributed. It adapts Shapley value theory, which is a way of dividing credit among people who jointly produce an outcome, so that the division can include blame as well as reward. The second move is economic. Workers participate through a dynamic stake pool, meaning some value is committed in advance and later adjusted. Adaptive dual-control parameters tune the balance between fairness and operating efficiency. In concrete terms, NAI tries to make the price of fraud visible while still letting useful workers earn and continue participating.
mech: The mechanism starts with a labeling task and a set of workers who produce answers for that task. For each worker, the system keeps evidence about ability, meaning how reliable that worker appears to be, and it also observes the current task result rather than judging only from a static profile. These ingredients enter the Ability-Result Characteristic Function. A characteristic function, in this setting, is a rule that says what value a group of workers appears to create for the labeling outcome. The paper extends this rule so value can be positive or negative. Next, a Shapley-style calculation asks a fairness question: if workers were added to the group in different possible orders, how much did this worker tend to change the outcome? A worker whose labels move the result toward quality receives positive contribution. A worker whose behavior damages the result receives negative contribution. That signed contribution then feeds the incentive side. The dynamic stake pool uses pre-commitment economics: workers have something at risk before final payment is settled. The adaptive controls change how strongly rewards and penalties are applied so the platform can punish harmful behavior without making the system too costly or hostile. The output is a payment and penalty decision tied to measured contribution, plus a higher-quality labeled dataset.
math: The first mathematical idea is cooperative credit assignment. When several people label the same data, the platform needs more than a count of who participated; it needs a fair estimate of each person's marginal effect, meaning the difference that person tends to make when added to others. Shapley value theory gives a disciplined way to divide credit by averaging a person's added value across many possible groupings. The paper changes the usual use by allowing the value to be signed. Positive numbers mean the worker helped; negative numbers mean the worker harmed the result. That matters because fraud is not merely absence of help. It can actively lower data quality. The second idea is a payoff rule with incentives. A payoff rule changes behavior because people react to expected reward and loss. Pre-commitment makes that loss credible: a worker has something at stake before the outcome is judged. The third idea is control under a tradeoff. The adaptive dual controls tune penalty and reward strength, balancing fairness against operational efficiency. Too little penalty leaves fraud cheap. Too much penalty treats noise as guilt and discourages participation. The math fits because the problem is not just classifying labels as right or wrong; it is assigning credit and blame among many contributors whose actions jointly determine a dataset.
dots: This paper connects crowdsourcing incentives to several recurring conference ideas. It belongs near fraud and anomaly detection because it treats harmful worker behavior as a pattern that must be made costly, not merely observed after damage is done. It also connects to fairness and responsible AI because the payment rule must avoid confusing low ability, task difficulty, and deliberate fraud; a punishment system that cannot make that distinction would be unfair even if it improves average quality. The Shapley value link places the paper in the broader family of contribution measurement, where systems ask how to divide credit among people, data sources, model components, or agents that jointly produce an outcome. Its economic side connects to mechanism design: instead of only predicting behavior, the system changes the rules of participation so honest labeling becomes more attractive than harmful labeling. The multimodal datasets show that the issue is not tied to one data type.
ww: The approach should work better than flat payment because it changes what workers are being paid for. A flat rule buys completed actions. NAI tries to buy useful contribution. If a worker's answer improves the task result, the signed contribution score can reward that effect. If the answer harms the result, the same scoring language can assign a negative value rather than pretending the worker merely contributed less. That is important because fraud is active damage. The stake pool then turns the score into an incentive before behavior happens: workers know that harmful contributions can cost them, so careless or fraudulent strategies become less attractive. At the same time, the ability-result design gives the system more evidence than a single wrong answer. It can combine a worker's ability with real-time task outcomes, which should reduce the chance that honest mistakes are punished like deliberate attacks. The abstract's reported gains across images, text, audio, and video suggest the mechanism is using a general property of crowdsourcing: quality improves when money follows measured contribution rather than task volume alone.
po: The payoff is a labeling market that can reward careful workers and penalize harmful contributors inside the same rule. The abstract reports extensive experiments on image, text, audio, and video datasets, including a 16.6% improvement in video labeling accuracy and a 33.9% reduction in fraudulent behavior against baselines. It also reports deployment on NetEase Youling, with 430,000 registered workers and 80,000 monthly active workers. In real-time A/B testing, NAI improved labeling quality by 59.6% for beginner tasks and reduced fraud rates by 14.8% to 33.9% across difficulty levels. The practical capability is better data quality without relying only on manual policing.
limits: Several assumptions have to hold. The system must estimate worker ability and task results well enough that signed contribution is meaningful. If the result signal is noisy, biased, or delayed, a good worker could be penalized or a harmful worker could escape cost. The stake pool must be acceptable to workers; otherwise the mechanism may improve quality among remaining workers while driving away useful participants. The abstract reports strong deployment evidence, but it does not show every detail of worker experience, appeal processes, long-term adaptation by fraudsters, or how penalties behave on rare hard tasks. The method also assumes money-based incentives are the right lever for the platform setting.
